content_voiceover: Two final questions from the 112th year exam. Question twenty four asks which statement about inherited protein S deficiency is wrong, and the answer is B, because protein S deficiency is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, not autosomal recessive, this is a classic point of confusion since so many coagulation deficiencies are recessive, but the natural anticoagulant deficiencies, antithrombin, protein C, and protein S, are all autosomal dominant. The other statements hold true, protein S is a vitamin K dependent cofactor for activated protein C, many patients previously labeled as protein S deficient actually have activated protein C resistance from factor five Leiden, up to a quarter of patients can have arterial events including stroke, and neonatal purpura fulminans along with warfarin induced skin necrosis are recognized associations. Question sixty three asks which clinical presentations suggest an underlying hypercoagulable state, and the answer is D, options three, four, and five, cerebral venous thrombosis, mesenteric or portal vein thrombosis, and recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis, these unusual site or recurrent presentations are the classic red flags for thrombophilia, whereas massive pulmonary embolism and postpartum thrombosis, options one and two, are common presentations that do not by themselves suggest an underlying hereditary hypercoagulable disorder.
keypoints: Protein S deficiency is autosomal DOMINANT, not recessive
Many prior protein S deficiency diagnoses are actually APC resistance from factor V Leiden
Up to 25% of protein S deficient patients have arterial events including stroke
Red flags for thrombophilia: cerebral venous, mesenteric/portal, or recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis
Massive PE and postpartum thrombosis alone do not specifically suggest thrombophilia
keypoint_voiceover: Remember protein S deficiency, like antithrombin and protein C deficiency, is autosomal dominant, not recessive. And the clinical clues that point toward an underlying hypercoagulable state are unusual-site or recurrent thromboses, cerebral venous, mesenteric or portal, and recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis, not simply a massive PE or postpartum clot.
